title: A regulator request through the secure world

steps.title: Powering the SD card takes a trip into the secure world
steps.body:
Six lanes, left to right: three Linux layers, then OP-TEE's monitor and SCMI server (both secure world) and the power chip. Time runs downward; teal arrows are the normal world, rose arrows the secure world, dashed arrows the return.

The example: the SD card driver needs its supply. SCMI is Arm's System Control and Management Interface, a message protocol; here it is carried by `smc`, the instruction that crosses into the secure world.

steps.title: 1. The SD card driver asks for its supply
steps.body: During `mmci_probe()` the driver asks the regulator framework for its `vmmc` supply. Without power the card cannot work, and the root filesystem is on that card.

steps.title: 2. The supply is an SCMI voltage domain
steps.body: The device tree says `vmmc-supply = <&scmi_v3v3>`. That regulator is not a driver for a chip Linux can reach: the power chip's I²C bus is disabled for Linux, so the regulator is an SCMI voltage domain, number `VOLTD_SCMI_STPMIC1_BUCK4`.

steps.title: 3. Linux sends an SCMI voltage-domain message
steps.body: The SCMI regulator driver builds a message for protocol `0x17`, voltage domain. The reply will carry a status.

steps.title: 4. The transport puts it in shared memory
steps.body: The `arm_scmi` OP-TEE transport opens a session to OP-TEE's pseudo trusted application for SCMI and hands over the message in a shared buffer.

steps.title: 5. An smc crosses into the secure world
steps.body: The `smc` instruction traps into the monitor, which is part of OP-TEE on this 32-bit chip. There is no separate BL31.

steps.title: 6. The monitor saves the normal world
steps.body: `sm_smc_entry` saves the normal-world context and runs OP-TEE's thread that serves the call.

steps.title: 7. The SCMI server finds the rail
steps.body: `pta/scmi.c` hands the message to the SCMI server, which looks the domain up in its table: the row for `buck4` is the rail named `v3v3`.

steps.title: 8. OP-TEE switches the rail
steps.body: OP-TEE's own driver talks to the STPMIC1 over I²C4 and enables the rail. The status goes back through the shared buffer and the `smc` returns.

steps.anchor: Why does a regulator need a round trip?
steps.title: Takeaway: this is why the SD card works here
steps.body: OP-TEE's STM32MP15 server serves voltage domains. The 64-bit board's STM32MP25 server serves clocks and resets only, so that board needs a workaround device tree; this one boots the stock tree.
